title: What is it to Seek and Speak the Truth in Love?
description: Welcome to part two of my five-part series on Intellectual Charity. The first part is here , though it isn’t necessary that you read it before you read this entry. In all areas of life, the Christian is called to the moral heights: turn the other cheek; go the extra mile. We are called to emulate Christ, who laid down his life for us while we were still at enmity with him. We hear parables that encourage us to go above and beyond the call of duty. Indeed, the technical term for such an act—an act that goes above and beyond the call of duty, like when a stranger saves a dying man found on the side of the road, taking him to an inn and paying for it with his own money—is supererogation , a word that comes to us from St. Jerome’s Vulgate translation of our Lord’s parable of the Good Samaritan. As the Samaritan says to the innkeeper, whatever more you spend ( supererogaveris ), I will repay you. So, it should be no surprise to us, then, that in seeking and speaking the truth, we Christians are called to a high standard. But what exactly is the standard? Just how high is it? Remember when Peter asked how many times he had to forgive his brother? You can hear him thinking he’s got a pretty high bar already when he says “seven.” And honestly, that is pretty high, isn’t it? Seven times for the same type of sin?! But recall our Lord’s answer of seventy -seven, or even seventy times seven. Is the bar for seeking and speaking the truth equally audaciously high? Thanks for reading Investigations by the Thomistic Institute! Subscribe for free to receive new posts every Monday.

title: Time in Science and Philosophy
description: Johannes Vermeer, “The Astronomer,: 1668, via Wikimedia Commons. Physicists who work in general relativity carry two very different definitions of time in their research. One is “proper” time, which is a measure of the amount of physical change that a system experiences. Proper time is what a clock measures. Carry a clock from event A to event B, and the number it displays is a direct observable that you can write down. A series of events for a given object is called its worldline. I might awake, drive into work, sit for four hours, drive to an airport, take a plane to the East Coast, and check into a hotel. My worldline has involved a series of events in which I am alternately stationary, moving at constant speed, accelerating, and rising a certain distance away from the center of the Earth. But the clock I take with me will display an elapsed time which anyone who reads it—even though they moved on a different worldline-- will agree upon. “Coordinate” time, on the other hand, is one of four coordinates assigned to events in the four-dimensional continuum called spacetime. Spacetime consists of three space-like dimensions and one time-like dimension in our universe. The path of any material entity through spacetime can be visualized as a series of events, which are linked together to form its world line. Coordinate time is a labeling of events that allows one to quantify the relationship between different worldlines. For example, if I play a three-minute song on my iPhone while on a plane, and an observer on the ground wants to know how long the song lasted by her reckoning, she must first assign times to the start and end events in her stationary reference frame, correcting for the travel time of the wireless signal from my airplane.

title: Outsourcing Your Intellect
description: Alexander Rothaug , “The Three Fates,” 1910, via Wikimedia Commons. All the world’s a stage, And all the men and women merely players; They have their exits and their entrances; And one man in his time plays many parts.” (William Shakespeare, As You Like It) Duc, o parens celsique dominator poli, Quocumque placuit ; nulla parendi mora est. Adsum inpiger. Fac nolle, comitabor gemens Malusque patiar, facere quod licuit bono. Ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt (Seneca, Moral Epistle 107 , n.11 Verses attributed to Cleanthes) The Problem of the Whispering Earring (or Bob’s Smart Glasses) Scott Alexander’s Whispering Earring imagines a magical earring that tells its wearer exactly what to do in every situation. He insists: the earring is always right . By “always right,” he does not mean that it makes the best possible decisions in every situation, but that it always makes a better decision than its wearer would have done, even after careful thought. I would like to introduce a modified version of the whispering earring for us to consider, but let’s change the earring into smart glasses to make it more true to the moment. Now let’s say the smart glasses interface with a perfect AGI model, so that their wearer, we shall call him Bob, can ask the model to supply him with answers to all questions relevant to daily life. Let’s say that one day Bob does not want to deliberate or think about his actions and decides that he will rely on his smart glasses for all of his decisions and tasks.
